newsitem.title: USA: Reno says FBI crime lab's impact to be determined.
newsitem.headline: Reno says FBI crime lab's impact to be determined.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said Thursday it was yet to be determined whether problems at the FBI's crime laboratory will undermine any criminal cases.

Commenting for the first time on the investigation by the Justice Department's inspector general into the laboratory, Reno said she wanted to wait for completion of his report before making any final judgments.
"We are continuing in that effort," she said, referring to department attempts to determine which cases might be affected. "When the report is completed, then we will complete our determination."

Asked at her weekly news briefing if her statement conflicted with FBI assurances that no criminal prosecutions would be compromised, Reno said, "I think we have just got to see as the conclusions are reached."
She added: "We just take each case on a case-by-case basis and make sure that we pursue each matter."
But departing Deputy FBI Director Weldon Kennedy, who has been in charge of dealing with the laboratory controversy, later repeated his prediction that no cases will be adversely affected.
"We are very confident that we are going to be able to overcome any and all criticism," he told a group of reporters. "We have the matter under control ... None of these cases will be jeopardised."
FBI Director Louis Freeh said many of the problems surrounding the laboratory already have been addressed, noting the process for it to be accredited had almost been concluded.

FBI officials have said a recent draft report by the inspector general sharply criticised the laboratory for poor management practices and sloppy handling of evidence. It raised questions about procedures and contaminated evidence.
But they denied the report found laboratory officials deliberately slanted their findings to favour prosecutors or were pressured by agents to lie about their conclusions.

Reno said she has heard "a lot that's been wrong" in media reports about the laboratory, but declined to elaborate. The still-secret report is expected to be finished and released in March at the earliest.

The FBI last week announced it had removed four officials from the laboratory in response to the investigation, including whistleblower Frederic Whitehurst, whose initial complaints triggered the inquiry that began in 1995.

Whitehurst may be called as a defence witness at the trial later this year of Oklahoma City bombing suspect Timothy McVeigh, and he testified as a defence witness in the World Trade Centre bombing case.
The FBI last week also said it was building a new crime lab as one of a number of steps aimed at improving its forensic unit. The $130 million facility is expected to be ready by 1999.

Reno was unable to estimate how many cases ultimately may be affected by shortcomings at the laboratory. But she said when problem cases have been identified, the Justice Department has attempted to make "all information available" to prosecutors and defence lawyers.
